title: Millions of Indians Live With Hepatitis B Without Knowing It as World Pushes to Break Down Barriers to Care
excerpt: Ahead of World Hepatitis Day on July 28, global health bodies and Indian experts are urging aggressive screening and treatment to reach the estimated 40 million carriers who remain undiagnosed.
body:
• India has an estimated 40 million hepatitis B carriers — the world's second-largest pool — with the majority undiagnosed
  • World Hepatitis Day 2026's theme, "Hepatitis: Let's Break It Down," calls for removing barriers to testing, treatment and prevention
  • India's National Viral Hepatitis Control Plan has screened over 75 lakh people and treated more than 71,000 free of cost since 2018
  • A recent hospital study found 3.1% of patients tested for unrelated conditions carried undiagnosed hepatitis B infections

A Silent Epidemic Hiding in Plain Sight

Every 30 seconds, someone in the world dies from complications linked to chronic hepatitis — cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer. In India, the numbers are staggering: an estimated 40 million people carry hepatitis B, making the country home to the world's second-largest pool of chronic infections after China. Most of them have no idea.

Ahead of World Hepatitis Day on July 28, the World Health Organization and Indian medical institutions are renewing calls to confront the disease with the urgency it demands. This year's global theme — "Hepatitis: Let's Break It Down" — is a direct appeal to dismantle the stigma, funding gaps and health system failures that keep millions from diagnosis and treatment.

"The tools needed to eliminate viral hepatitis already exist," the WHO said in its 2026 campaign statement. "Effective vaccines, accurate diagnostics, curative treatments for hepatitis C, and lifelong therapies for hepatitis B can prevent infections, save lives, and reduce liver cancer and cirrhosis."

India's Progress and Persistent Gaps

"This year's global theme — "Hepatitis: Let's Break It Down" — is a direct appeal to dismantle the stigma, funding gaps and health system failures that keep millions from diagnosis and treatment."

India was the first country in the WHO South-East Asia Region to launch a comprehensive national hepatitis programme. Under the National Viral Hepatitis Control Plan, launched in 2018, more than 75 lakh people have been screened for hepatitis B and C at government-run facilities — entirely free of cost. Over 71,000 patients have received treatment, also at no charge.

The country has also become a global leader in producing and mass-procuring direct-acting antiviral drugs that can cure most hepatitis C cases in a 12-to-24-week course. Tens of thousands of patients have already benefited.

But the scale of the challenge dwarfs these efforts. With a carrier rate estimated between 2% and 4% of the general population, the vast majority of infected individuals have never been tested. A recent cross-sectional study at a tertiary care hospital in central India found that 3.1% of patients presenting for conditions entirely unrelated to hepatitis tested positive for hepatitis B — and most had no idea they were infected.

A separate study screening over 13,800 asymptomatic healthcare workers and surgical patients found a 2.57% hepatitis B positivity rate. Nearly half of those who tested positive but were negative for the hepatitis B e-antigen still carried significant viral loads capable of transmitting the infection and causing liver damage.

Why the Disease Stays Hidden

Hepatitis B and C rarely produce symptoms in their early stages. The virus can silently damage the liver for years or even decades before clinical signs — fatigue, abdominal swelling, jaundice — appear. By then, cirrhosis or cancer may have already set in.

Experts say over 75% of Indians are unaware that a disease like hepatitis exists. The states most affected include Punjab, Haryana, Odisha, Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, according to the All India Institute of Medical Sciences. An estimated four lakh people die from hepatitis-related liver diseases in India every year.

Stigma compounds the problem. Hepatitis B is sometimes conflated with lifestyle choices or confused with hepatitis A, a milder, food-borne illness. Fear of social consequences keeps people from seeking tests, and underfunded rural health centres often lack the diagnostic capacity to identify carriers even when they do show up.

A Global Push Toward 2030 Elimination

The WHO has set an ambitious target: eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. To mark the 2026 campaign, a high-level event — organised by the Government of Brazil and the WHO — will bring together ministers, policymakers and affected communities on the sidelines of the 26th International AIDS Conference to identify concrete steps toward that goal.

The campaign calls for stronger political commitment, sustained investment and expanded equitable access to prevention, testing and treatment. For India, that means scaling screening beyond hospital walls and into community health programmes, strengthening birth-dose vaccination coverage for hepatitis B and ensuring antiviral treatments reach patients in smaller towns and rural areas.

What Families Should Know

Hepatitis B vaccination is available for both children and adults. For those already infected, affordable treatments can suppress the virus and prevent liver damage. Hepatitis C, once considered incurable, can now be eliminated from the body entirely with a short course of oral medication.

Health experts urge anyone with a family history of liver disease, those who have undergone blood transfusions or surgeries, and people from high-prevalence regions to get tested. For the Indian diaspora, a conversation about screening during family visits home could be the difference between early treatment and a late-stage diagnosis.
nri_angle: Indian diaspora members with family in India should be aware of the massive undiagnosed hepatitis B burden and encourage screening during visits home.
author: Diaspora Desk
